history.contentIn: The Stratospheric Controlled Perturbation Experiment (SCoPEx) was a proposed research initiative by Harvard University aimed at investigating the behavior of aerosol particles in the stratosphere. Principal investigator Frank Keutsch, along with colleagues including David Keith, publicly introduced the concept at the American Geophysical Union Fall Meeting in 2017. The experiment was intended to enhance computer models for assessing the risks and benefits of solar geoengineering, specifically solar radiation management, rather than testing geoengineering deployment or cooling the planet. It involved a scientific balloon gondola designed to operate at approximately 20 km altitude, releasing a very small quantity of material—around 100 grams to less than 2 kg, primarily calcium carbonate—into a defined volume of the atmosphere. A 2021 hardware test in Sweden, conducted in collaboration with the Swedish Space Corporation, was halted by the SCoPEx Advisory Committee pending societal engagement, and no particles were released. In March 2024, it was announced that Keutsch would no longer pursue SCoPEx, and the platform is expected to be redirected for unrelated stratospheric research.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) identifies SAI as the most researched solar geoengineering method, with the potential to moderate warming at moderate intensities, though it may have unintended consequences if improperly managed. Materials considered for SAI include sulfates and, occasionally, calcite, delivered via specialized high-altitude aircraft. Currently, there is no global operational deployment of SAI. It is crucial to understand that SAI does not remove carbon dioxide or alleviate ocean acidification and necessitates continuous action to counteract persistent high emissions. Associated risks include potential impacts on ozone chemistry, changes in precipitation patterns, and governance challenges. history.contentIn: The Paris Agreement is a legally binding international treaty on climate change adopted by 196 Parties at COP21 in Paris on 12 December 2015 and in force from 4 November 2016. Its central aim is to hold the increase in the global average temperature to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit the increase to 1.5°C. Parties submit nationally determined contributions (NDCs) describing their mitigation plans; the Agreement uses a ratchet mechanism of successive NDCs rather than a single top-down allocation of tonnes. The treaty does not ban talking about geoengineering, but it is not a secret authorisation to spray the atmosphere. Article 4 addresses peaking of greenhouse gas emissions and a balance between anthropogenic emissions by sources and removals by sinks in the second half of the century (often discussed as net-zero CO2). The United States joined, withdrew under the first Trump administration, and rejoined under the Biden administration; participation has been politically contested but the scientific case for rapid emissions cuts is independent of any one administration. Meeting Paris temperature goals requires deep, sustained cuts in fossil CO2, methane and other greenhouse gases, plus protection of carbon sinks — not covert aviation spraying.
